final_proof:
The claim as stated is false because no surjectivity hypothesis is imposed.

Counterexample. Let X={∗} be the one-point space, let Y={0}∪{1/n:n∈N, n≥1} with the subspace topology inherited from R, and define f(∗)=0. The space X is compact and locally connected, Y is Hausdorff, and f is continuous. However, Y is not locally connected at 0. Indeed, every connected subset of Y is a singleton: if C⊆Y contained distinct points a<b, choose c∈(a,b)\Y; then C∩(−∞,c) and C∩(c,∞) would be disjoint, nonempty, relatively open subsets separating C. Thus the only connected subset of Y containing 0 is {0}, while {0} is not open in Y (every neighborhood of 0 contains 1/n for all sufficiently large n). Hence 0 has no connected open neighborhood, so Y is not locally connected.

The correct statement is: if X is compact and locally connected, Y is Hausdorff, and f:X→Y is continuous, then the image f(X), with its subspace topology, is locally connected. In particular, the original conclusion is valid if f is also assumed surjective.

We first record a useful criterion. Suppose a space Z has the following property: for every z∈Z and every open set V containing z, there is a connected neighborhood N of z such that N⊆V, where neighborhood means that N contains an open set containing z. Then Z is locally connected. To prove this, let C be the connected component of V containing z. The given N is a connected subset of V meeting C, so maximality of the component gives N⊆C. More generally, for every p∈C the same property gives a connected neighborhood N_p of p contained in V. Since N_p meets C at p, C∪N_p is connected, whence N_p⊆C. Each p∈C therefore has an open neighborhood contained in C, so C is open. Thus z has the connected open neighborhood C contained in V, proving local connectedness.

Now put Z=f(X) with the subspace topology and regard f as a surjection g:X→Z. The space Z is Hausdorff. Moreover, g is a closed map: if F is closed in X, then F is compact, so g(F) is compact, and every compact subset of the Hausdorff space Z is closed.

Fix z∈Z and an open neighborhood V of z in Z. Let K=g^{-1}({z}). Since {z} is closed in Z, K is a closed subset of the compact space X and hence is compact. Also K⊆g^{-1}(V). For every x∈K, local connectedness of X supplies a connected open set U_x such that x∈U_x⊆g^{-1}(V). By compactness of K, finitely many of these sets, say U_1,…,U_m, cover K. Set A=U_1∪⋯∪U_m. Each g(U_i) is connected and contains z, because U_i was chosen about a point of K. Consequently B=g(A)=g(U_1)∪⋯∪g(U_m) is connected, as it is a union of connected sets having the common point z. Also B⊆V.

It remains to verify that B is a neighborhood of z; we do not assume that a continuous map sends open sets to open sets. Since A is open, X\A is closed, and closedness of g implies that g(X\A) is closed in Z. Because A contains the entire fiber K, z∉g(X\A). Therefore W=Z\g(X\A) is an open neighborhood of z. Furthermore W⊆g(A)=B: if w∈W, surjectivity of g gives x∈X with g(x)=w, and x cannot lie in X\A, so x∈A. Thus B is a connected neighborhood of z contained in V. The criterion just proved applies at every z and V, and hence Z=f(X) is locally connected. If f is surjective onto Y, then Z=Y, yielding the corrected conclusion.
